beats.headline: Why do your tests take 20 minutes to run?
beats.subline: If you are chasing 100% line coverage, you are likely testing the wrong things.
beats.narration: If your test suite takes twenty minutes to run, you have a problem. Chasing 100% line coverage is a trap. You need a balanced trophy, not a pyramid.

beats.title: The Testing Trophy
beats.subtitle: Focus on boundaries, not just logic

nodes.label: Unit Tests
nodes.detail: Fast domain logic, no Spring context

beats.narration: The trophy model prioritizes fast unit tests for domain rules, while shifting integration effort to infrastructure boundaries like SQL queries and HTTP contracts.

beats.title: Unit vs. Integration
beats.narration: Unit tests should be lightning fast, testing domain math without booting Spring. Integration tests use Testcontainers to verify real DB behavior, catching bugs H2 misses.

beats.title: AssertJ for Precision

steps.explanation: isEqualTo checks scale, failing on 10.0 vs 10.00. Use isEqualByComparingTo for numeric value equality.

beats.narration: Always use AssertJ. For BigDecimals, never use isEqualTo, as it checks scale. Use isEqualByComparingTo to compare the actual numeric value.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Mocking strategies and avoiding the over-mocking trap →
beats.narration: That is the foundation. In Part 2, we look at Mockito and why mocking everything is actually a technical debt nightmare.

beats.headline: Are you mocking your own domain objects?
beats.subline: If your tests break every time you refactor, you are over-mocking.
beats.narration: If you mock every single helper service, your tests become brittle mirrors of your code. If you change the implementation, you break the test, even if the public behavior is identical.

beats.title: Mockito Best Practices

steps.explanation: MockitoExtension enables strict stubbing—unused stubs cause failures, preventing test rot.

beats.narration: Use MockitoExtension for strict stubbing. It forces you to clean up unused stubs, keeping your tests lean and preventing silent failures.

beats.title: @WebMvcTest Slice
beats.subtitle: Test controllers without the full app
beats.narration: WebMvcTest boots only the web layer. Use MockMvc to fire requests and MockitoBean to swap out your services. It is fast and isolates your API contracts.

beats.title: Spring Boot 3.4+ Note
beats.narration: If you are on Spring Boot 3.4 or higher, stop using MockBean. Switch to the new MockitoBean annotation from the Spring Framework 6.2 package.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Testcontainers and the @ServiceConnection magic →
beats.narration: Mocking is for I/O, not logic. In Part 3, we use Testcontainers to run real databases without the manual configuration headache.

beats.headline: H2 is lying to your tests.
beats.subline: Production uses Postgres, but your tests use H2? You are missing critical SQL bugs.
beats.narration: H2 is not Postgres. It ignores JSONB operators, native arrays, and transaction isolation levels. If your production DB is Postgres, your tests must run on Postgres.

beats.title: Zero-Boilerplate Containers

steps.explanation: Automatically injects JDBC connection details into Spring, removing the need for DynamicPropertySource.

beats.narration: ServiceConnection is a game changer. It automatically wires your container's dynamic port into your Spring context. No more manual property overrides.

beats.title: Container Reuse Pattern
beats.narration: Do not start a container per class. Use an abstract base class to share one singleton container. It saves seconds per test class and keeps your build fast.

beats.title: Cleanup Strategy
beats.narration: Avoid DirtiesContext at all costs. It destroys your Spring context cache, forcing a full reboot. Clean your DB state with batch deletes instead.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): The @Transactional trap and final performance tips →
beats.narration: Containers are non-negotiable. In Part 4, we reveal the hidden transaction bugs that make your tests pass locally but fail in production.

beats.headline: Why @Transactional is killing your integration tests.
beats.subline: It hides lazy-loading bugs and makes your tests see ghosts.
beats.narration: Transactional on a test method feels convenient, but it hides lazy-loading exceptions and creates phantom data issues when using random ports.

beats.title: The Threading Problem
beats.subtitle: Why RANDOM_PORT breaks @Transactional
beats.narration: When using random port, the test and the server run on different threads. The server cannot see your uncommitted test data, leading to false negatives.

beats.title: The Better Way

steps.explanation: Manually clearing the DB ensures you test real commit/flush cycles, not just rolled-back memory state.

beats.narration: Skip the transactional annotation on integration tests. Manually clean your database in AfterEach. This forces your code to handle real commits and flushes.

beats.title: Performance Checklist
beats.narration: Follow this checklist to keep your build times under two minutes. Consistent configuration ensures Spring reuses your context cache effectively.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You have mastered automated testing. Check out the roadmap link for the full lab and verify your test suites today.
